Case Explorer — The Gambia v. Myanmar

Application of the Genocide Convention · ICJ Merits Judgment, 19 November 2026

By a 9–6 vote—and for the first time without prior international criminal convictions—the International Court of Justice held a State responsible for committing genocide. The Court revisited Bosnia v. Serbia (2007) on the duty to prevent (¶487), set out a structured evidentiary framework for UN investigative dossiers and open-source material, and built cross-bloc majorities (10–5 to 14–1) on investigation, punishment, domestic legislation, reparations, and provisional measures.

Section III · Substantive & Procedural Holdings

Five Core Legal Issues

Side-by-side comparison of Majority holdings, concurring refinements, and dissenting critiques across the five doctrinal and evidentiary axes of the Judgment.

01

Genocidal Intent (Dolus Specialis): Coexistence & Holistic Inference

Retains “only reasonable inference” while clarifying concurrent military motives and contextual proof.

9–6 · Clause (1)
Majority Holding

No threshold “pattern of conduct” is required (¶386–389); the Court weighs context, hate speech, targeting of children, sexual violence, and scale holistically (¶397). Under ¶443, genocidal intent may coexist with military or displacement aims unless mutually incompatible; attacks on fleeing civilians and village bulldozing negate mere expulsion (¶451–467).

Separate & Concurring

Pres. Iwasawa and Judge Brant emphasize continuity with Croatia and Tolimir. Judge Charlesworth argues diffuse collective State intent cannot follow criminal-trial checklists, while Judge Tladi questions excluding dolus eventualis.

Dissenting Views

Joint Dissent & VP Sebutinde contend treating motives as compatible lowers Croatia, citing safe-passage evidence, unexploited opportunities to destroy, and ARSA counter-insurgency. Nolte & Kress warn against expanding “foundations of the group.”

Implication Parties pleading genocidal intent must show why the totality of conduct exceeds any security or displacement aim, while proactively rebutting defense evidence of safe-passage corridors and unexploited opportunities.
02

Article I Duty to Prevent: Departure from Bosnia (2007)

Breach of the duty to prevent is no longer conditioned on a merits finding that genocide occurred.

9–6 · Clause (2)
Majority Holding

Expressly departing from Bosnia (2007, ¶431), the Court holds in ¶487 that responsibility for failing to prevent genocide does not depend on proof that genocide actually took place. Myanmar breached Art. I by manifestly failing to use available means against a serious risk (¶471–488).

Cross-Bloc Endorsement

In a landmark cross-bloc opinion, Majority Cleveland & dissenting ad hoc Kress defend ¶487: Art. I is an autonomous obligation of conduct, not an ILC Art. 14(3) obligation of result. Brant, Hmoud, and Tladi cite the 1948 travaux préparatoires.

Dissenting Views

Judge Tomka calls ¶487 a “revolution” violating ILC Art. 14(3). Judge Abraham notes neither Party asked to overrule Bosnia and warns of reduced legal certainty; Nolte & Sebutinde caution against speculative “serious-risk” claims.

Implication An Applicant can now establish a merits breach of Art. I—under the “high level of certainty” standard—by proving actual or constructive knowledge of a serious risk and failure to deploy available means, even without proving completed genocide.
03

Evidentiary Assessment: UN Mechanisms, OSINT & Corfu Channel

Establishes how the Court weighs UN dossiers, open-source forensics, and State non-co-operation absent criminal verdicts.

Evidentiary Protocol
Majority Holding

Without prior tribunal verdicts, the Court gives considerable weight to IIMM reports & signed statements (¶95, 116), Meta/Facebook military attribution (¶161–168), UNOSAT & GPS-tagged AV (¶121, 228, 279–281), and corroborated FFM findings (¶105–112). Access refusal + 26 unanswered IIMM requests support Corfu Channel inferences (¶128–131).

Separate & Concurring

Gómez Robledo & Hmoud reject ¶130’s “no general duty” rule, arguing UN Charter Arts. 2(5) & 55–56 mandate good-faith co-operation. Aurescu cautions against adopting third-party discrimination labels uncritically.

Dissenting Views

VP Sebutinde warns reading ¶131 with ¶109 shifts the burden of proof, challenging opaque FFM sourcing, unsigned LAW summaries (CK0206), and redactions. Xue documents cross-annex witness duplication; Nolte & Kress critique circular corroboration and AAR discounting.

Implication Digital forensics, satellite imagery, and UN investigative dossiers can sustain a genocide merits case when metadata are authenticated, witnesses are de-duplicated across annexes, and non-co-operation is systematically documented.
04

Protected Group, Actus Reus (Art. II(a)–(d)) & Humanitarian Law

Finds Arts. II(a), II(b), and II(d) established, holds Art. II(c) unproven, and rejects IHL as lex specialis.

Art. II(a)(b)(d) ✓ · II(c) ✕
Majority Holding

Recognizes Rohingya as a distinct ethnic group (¶308–310). Finds Art. II(a) killing (¶312–319), Art. II(b) bodily/mental harm incl. sexual violence (¶320–337), and Art. II(d) preventing births via marriage/birth limits & sexual violence (¶357–371), while finding Art. II(c) “slow death” unproven (¶338–356). Rejects IHL lex specialis (¶296–305).

Separate & Concurring

Gómez Robledo dissents on Art. II(c): reconciling authentic FR/EN/ES texts (devant entraîner / calculated / hayan de acarrear, VCLT Art. 33(4)), camp confinement, denied healthcare & 700k+ displacement constitute “slow death.” Cleveland & Tladi unpack physical vs. social destruction.

Dissenting Views

ad hoc Kress concurs in rejecting IHL lex specialis, but joins Nolte in warning that stretching Art. II(b) mental harm to displacement conflates ethnic cleansing with genocide. Sebutinde & Tomka enforce strict Art. IX jurisdictional boundaries.

Implication IHL lex specialis objections failed across blocs. Art. II(c) requires proof of objective capability to cause physical “slow death,” while Arts. II(b) and II(d) now carry detailed ICJ evidentiary precedent.
05

Remedies, Erga Omnes Compensation & Provisional Measure 3

Orders victim-oriented restitution and a Phase 2 compensation process, alongside bench splits on quantum mechanics.

10–5 / 11–4 · Clauses (9)–(12)
Majority Holding

Orders comprehensive restitution (¶615, safe return & non-discrimination), affirms a duty to compensate Rohingya victims (10–5), sets a 2-year reporting/negotiation window before Phase 2 quantum (10–5), and finds breach of 2020 PM3 on evidence preservation (11–4, ¶646(12)).

Majority Split on Phase 2

Pres. Iwasawa & Aurescu vote against Clause (11): a non-injured erga omnes Applicant lacks capacity to quantify individual victim losses; Aurescu proposes an independent Claims Commission. Brant & Pillay urge explicit citizenship guarantees in the dispositif.

Dissenting & Cross-Bloc

Abraham critiques ¶615(5) under ILC Art. 35 (restitution cannot remedy pre-existing discrimination). Tomka joins Majority across (9)–(12); Abraham & Kress cross over to support Clause (11) Phase 2 (and Kress joins Clause (12) PM3).

Implication Non-injured erga omnes Applicants can win victim restitution, compensation, and PM breach findings, but should propose a Claims Commission or trust-fund valuation mechanism early and tie restitution strictly to wrongful-act causation.
Section IV · Evidentiary Standards

Hierarchy of Evidentiary Weight

Probative weight assigned by the Court absent prior criminal tribunal findings, paired with principal bench critiques. Click any tier to open filtered Explorer rulings.

Tier & Probative Weight
Evidentiary Categories & Key Rulings
Bench Objections & Limits
Live cross-examined witnesses (¶87–88), signed IIMM statements & analytical reports verified to criminal-law standards (¶93–96, 116), Meta/Facebook forensic network attribution (¶161–168), and UNOSAT geospatial / GPS-tagged AV analysis (¶121, 228, 279–281).
Dissent critique: Oral witnesses observe narrow village slices (Nolte ¶20); IIMM records include safe-passage accounts (Joint Dissent ¶50) and cross-annex witness overlap (Xue ¶1–43).
UN Fact-Finding Mission (FFM) factual findings corroborated by primary or geospatial evidence despite its lower mandate threshold (¶105–112), undisputed press reports of senior military speeches (¶156), and liberal Corfu Channel inferences following territorial refusal and 26 unanswered IIMM requests (¶79, 128–131).
Dissent critique: Sebutinde and Nolte challenge opaque FFM sourcing and circular UN/NGO corroboration, and warn that reading ¶109 with ¶131 risks shifting the burden of proof.
NGO dossiers (lower weight than UN bodies; never standalone proof, ¶123–124), redacted witness statements (admissible with reduced weight, ¶89–92), unsigned third-party summaries (LAW CK0206, ¶93–96), late web-linked domestic inquiry annexes (ICOE) (¶126), and uncorroborated military/State reports & AARs (¶125).
Dissent critique: Sebutinde and Xue argue unilateral redactions impair adversarial testing, unsigned summaries fail Croatia ¶196, and discounting contemporaneous AARs creates asymmetry.
Legal assessments & genocide characterizations by UN fact-finders, Special Rapporteurs, or UNGA/HRC resolutions (factual findings may count; legal conclusions carry zero weight, ¶97–104), party-commissioned experts opining beyond technical expertise on ultimate legal issues (¶127), and unverified single-source hearsay.
Bench consensus: Both Majority and Dissent strictly exclude external legal conclusions—expert filings should remain confined to technical and forensic methodology.

Legal Issue Majority Judgment (9–6) Separate / Progressive Concurrences Dissenting Bloc (6 Judges)
1. Coexistence of Intent & Alternative Motives Genocidal intent may coexist with military/security aims if not incompatible (¶443); attacks on fleeing civilians negate mere displacement (¶451–467).
 Iwasawa defends continuity with ICTs; Hmoud says genocide can serve counter-terrorism; Tladi challenges excluding dolus eventualis; Brant (EN/FR) sees continuity.
 6-Judge Joint Dissent & Sebutinde: treating motives as "compatible" lowers Croatia; displacement, ARSA suppression & collective punishment remain open + unexploited opportunities.
2. Holistic Inference, Tolimir & "Foundations" Intent may be inferred holistically from context, hate speech, targeting & scale without prior "pattern of conduct" (¶386–389, 438–442).
 Charlesworth explains diffuse collective State intent cannot use a rigid checklist; Iwasawa aligns holistic factors with Tolimir.
 Joint Dissent calls "violating foundations" overly vague; Sebutinde says Tolimir can't cure weak evidence; Nolte & Kress critique cumulative expansion & collective State policy.
3. Standard of Proof ("Fully Conclusive") "Fully conclusive" for Art. III; "high level of certainty" for Arts. I/IV/VI; statutory interpretation for Art. V (¶80).
 Charlesworth questions importing criminal-trial "fully conclusive" bar into State responsibility.
 Sebutinde, Xue & Tomka insist absence of ICTY convictions demands heightened adherence to "fully conclusive" proof, not softening.
4. Corfu Channel & Duty to Co-operate With UN States generally need not grant UN access (¶130), but refusal + 26 unanswered IIMM requests allow liberal inferences without satisfactory explanation (¶128–131).
 Hmoud & Gómez Robledo (EN/FR) go further: reject "no general duty" rule—UN Members owe an affirmative duty to co-operate with UN fact-finding on plausible genocide.
 Sebutinde warns reading ¶131 with ¶109 creates a de facto burden shift; States may refuse UN bodies over neutrality/methodology concerns.
5. FFM, IIMM, OSINT & Military / ICOE Records IIMM reports (incl. Facebook OSINT) earn considerable weight (¶116, 161–168); FFM reliable when corroborated (¶105–112); NGOs lower weight; late ICOE links limited (¶126).
 Tladi notes fact-intensive witness/evidence weighing; Aurescu flags loose third-party discrimination labels.
 Sebutinde, Xue, Nolte & Kress: non-judicial thresholds earn no presumptive weight; opaque FFM sourcing & circular corroboration; discounting military AARs & ICOE annexes causes asymmetry.
6. Redacted Witnesses, Duplication & Unsigned Summaries Redactions reduce weight without barring admission; IIMM signed statements carry considerable weight; unsigned LAW accounts used rarely if corroborated (¶89–96).
 Majority judges generally endorsed the Judgment’s differentiated weighting protocol alongside oral testimony. Xue documents concrete cross-source duplication across LAW/IIMM annexes; Sebutinde critiques unilateral Party redactions & unsigned LAW CK0206; Joint Dissent cites IIMM safe-passage accounts.
7. Duty to Prevent Reversal (Maj. ¶487) Reverses Bosnia 2007: breach of Art. I duty to prevent is not conditioned on a finding that genocide actually occurred (¶487).
 Cleveland & ad hoc Kress (cross-bloc!), Hmoud, Tladi & Brant (EN/FR) vigorously defend autonomous due-diligence prevention triggered by serious risk.
 Tomka ("revolution" violating ILC Art. 14(3)), Abraham (EN/FR), Nolte ("outright reversal") & Sebutinde (¶20) insist completed genocide is an indispensable predicate.
8. Art. II(c) "Slow Death" & Art. II(d) Birth Prevention Finds Art. II(a)/(b)/(d) established, including birth/marriage decrees & sexual violence (¶357–371), but finds Art. II(c) conditions of life unproven (¶338–356).
 Gómez Robledo (EN/FR) disagrees sharply on Art. II(c): prolonged IDP camps, restricted healthcare & 700,000+ displacement establish objective "slow death."
 Nolte & Sebutinde warn stretching Art. II(b) serious mental harm to displacement trauma blurs ethnic cleansing with physical/biological genocide.
9. IHL Lex Specialis, "Destroy" & Art. IX Scope Rejects IHL as lex specialis (¶296–305); defines Rohingya as protected ethnic group (¶308–310); clarifies physical/biological destruction (¶288–293).
 Cleveland & Tladi elucidate destroying the "group, as such" beyond bare body counts.
 Kress concurs in rejecting IHL lex specialis & single-act actus reus (¶89–129) while insisting on collective State policy; Sebutinde & Tomka police strict Art. IX limits.
10. Erga Omnes Remedies, Phase 2 & 2020 PM3 Orders restitution (¶615), compensation & Phase 2 within 2 years (10–5), and finds breach of 2020 PM3 evidence preservation (11–4, ¶646(12)).
 Iwasawa & Aurescu dissent on Phase 2 quantum by The Gambia (Aurescu proposes claims commission); Brant/Pillay want explicit citizenship guarantees in dispositif.
 Kress (and Tomka) cross over to endorse victim reparation principle, Phase 2 & PM3 breach (11–4), while Nolte concurs on punishment (11–4) but dissents on PM3 & reparations.

1. Three-Tiered Standards of Proof Maj. ¶80 • Charlesworth ¶11–22 • Sebutinde ¶18–23

Convention ObligationApplicable StandardFull Bench Spectrum
Article III Acts
(Genocide, conspiracy, incitement, attempt, complicity)		 "Fully conclusive" Reaffirmed by Majority (¶80). Charlesworth (¶11–22) questions importing criminal-law proof into State responsibility; Sebutinde, Xue, Nolte & Tomka insist absence of ICTY convictions makes strict adherence mandatory.
Articles I, IV, VI
(Prevent, investigate, punish)		 "High level of certainty" Landmark shift (Maj. ¶487): Majority + Cleveland/Kress + Hmoud/Tladi/Brant decouple Art. I prevention breach from completed genocide. Tomka, Abraham, Nolte & Sebutinde dissent against reversing Bosnia 2007.
Article V
(Domestic legislation)		 Statutory interpretation 14–1 finding of breach & order to enact (Clauses 5 & 6); Judge Xue cast the lone dissent on both.

2. Burden Flexibility, Co-operation & Corfu Channel Maj. ¶79, 128–131 • Hmoud ¶2–9 • Gómez Robledo ¶27–40 • Sebutinde ¶61–66

Majority (¶79, 128–131): Burden stays on Applicant but applies flexibly; refusing access to UN bodies + 26 unanswered IIMM requests unlocks liberal factual inferences where Respondent offers no "satisfactory and convincing explanation."

Bench Split: Hmoud & Gómez Robledo (EN/FR) argue UN Member States have an affirmative duty to co-operate with UN fact-finding on plausible genocide. Sebutinde & Xue warn that treating non-rebuttal (¶109 + ¶131) as affirmative proof creates an impermissible de facto burden shift.

3. "Only Reasonable Inference", Coexistence & Dolus Specialis Maj. ¶386–389, 443, 451–467 • 6-Judge Joint Dissent • Iwasawa ¶1–10 • Tladi ¶24–33

Majority (9–6, ¶443): Genocidal intent may coexist with military/security motives if not incompatible, inferred holistically from context, speeches, targeting, and scale without a prior "pattern of conduct" finding. President Iwasawa defends this as continuous with Tolimir; Judge Tladi would even allow dolus eventualis.

6-Judge Joint Dissent (Sebutinde, Tomka, Abraham, Xue, Nolte, Kress): Argues treating alternative motives as "compatible" rather than "competing" departs from Croatia; ARSA counter-insurgency, forced displacement, and collective punishment—paired with limited scope and unexploited opportunities—preclude genocidal intent from being the only reasonable inference.
